Consult Summary:
- New, severe, three-day headache with photophobia and transient visual phenomena; working impression favors migraine-type headache, with secondary etiologies considered (CVST, IIH). Neuro exam and fundoscopy planned; analgesia adjusted and follow-up arranged; red-flag instructions provided.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Blinding headache started waking up three days ago; constant and disabling (peak ~8/10, improving to ~5/10 with time). Limited relief with ibuprofen.
- Headache characteristics: Diffuse pain with right-eye emphasis; photophobia (lights worsen pain); occasional visual symptoms described as flashing/shooting lights; no focal weakness, numbness, speech disturbance.
- Associated symptoms: Nausea without vomiting; no fever; no cough, nasal symptoms, or sinuses pain; no neck stiffness reported.
- Temporal pattern: Present most of the time for three days; better somewhat with NSAIDs but persistent; sleeps through the night, but headache may wake in the morning.
- Triggers/exposures: Estrogen-containing oral contraceptive pill for about one year; daily ibuprofen and paracetamol PRN; no smoking; alcohol about weekly.
- Past medical history: Childhood headaches; no chronic headaches otherwise; no known drug allergies.
- Family history: Mother has migraines.
- Social: Lives alone, works from home.
- Review of systems: No weight loss; fatigue possibly related to ongoing pain; no fevers or systemic signs.
- Medications: Combined oral contraceptive pill; ibuprofen; paracetamol as needed.
- Allergies: None reported.

Examination:
- Vitals: Not provided in transcript.
- Neurological/ophthalmologic: No exam results documented yet; plan includes a neurological examination and fundoscopy of the eyes.
- Other: No documented focal neurologic deficits or meningismus in the transcript.

Impression:
- Working clinical impression: Migraine-type headache with migrainous features is most likely given unilateral/right-eye emphasis, photophobia, visual phenomena, female patient with new onset headache affecting function, and partial response to NSAIDs.
- Differential considerations (prioritized):
  1) Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (CVST) related to estrogen-containing OCP — medium likelihood; risk factor present; headache is new and persistent; need imaging to rule out.
  2) Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (IIH) — medium likelihood; typical in young to middle-aged women with headaches and possible visual symptoms; fundoscopy necessary for papilledema.
  3) Intracranial mass or raised ICP — low likelihood given short 3-day course but included because of persistent, morning-predominant headache; imaging considered if red flags or progression.
  4) Meningitis/encephalitis — low likelihood without fever, meningismus, or altered mental status.
- Note on transcript vs. DDx: Transcript supports migraine as the leading diagnosis; DDx provides appropriate secondary considerations consistent with the presentation. No conflicting data requiring reversal of the primary impression.

Plan:
- Acute management:
  - Switch from ibuprofen to a stronger NSAID alternative for headache relief; continue paracetamol as adjunct; take medications with food.
- Diagnostic and follow-up actions:
  - Schedule a full neurological examination and fundoscopy (back-of-eye assessment) as soon as possible.
  - Book follow-up appointment via support line; if symptoms settle earlier, the visit can be canceled.
  - Blood pressure check performed at the appointment to reassess suitability of migraine treatment with OCP; review need to change hormonal therapy if migrainous features persist.
  - If headaches worsen, persist, or evolve (e.g., new fever, neck stiffness, focal deficits, altered consciousness, severe vomiting), go to A&E for urgent assessment.
- Additional considerations:
  - Discuss potential change of OCP if migrainous features persist; ongoing use may influence migraine patterns.
  - If imaging is pursued (to evaluate CVST or IIH), coordinate per clinician evaluation and results.
  - If specialist referral becomes necessary, referral via support team following full exam.
- Education for patient:
  - Explain red-flag symptoms requiring urgent care.
  - Emphasize taking medications with food.
  - Advise on monitoring for new neurological signs and report promptly.

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Vital signs (blood pressure, heart rate) were not documented; no actual neurological or fundoscopy findings available yet.
  - No imaging results available yet; no formal ophthalmologic exam results documented.
  - No explicit allergies beyond “none,” though documented in history.
- Conflicts:
  - No explicit conflicts between transcript and DDx; Migraine is supported; DDx appropriately includes secondary causes to consider.
- Transcript quality:
  - Generally clear; some data (vital signs, exam findings) were not provided in the transcript and will be obtained in the planned exam.

Notes:
- If imaging demonstrates no secondary cause, management can continue as migraine-focused care with lifestyle and preventive strategies as indicated.
- Follow-up plan may be adapted based on exam findings and imaging results.
